name: Kigali Genocide Memorial — Gisozi, Gasabo
type: National Memorial & UNESCO World Heritage Site
desc: The principal national memorial and final resting place for over 250,000 victims. Three permanent exhibitions document the genocide, a children's memorial, and a comparative exhibition on global genocidal violence.

testimony.text: We hid for weeks. When it was finally over and we emerged, the streets were silent. Everyone was gone. I walked through neighborhoods I had known my whole life and recognized nothing. The memorial gives them a place — a name, a grave, dignity. Without it, the world would forget them. I will not let them be forgotten.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor testimony, Kigali Genocide Memorial archives

context: Opened on the tenth anniversary of the genocide in April 2004, the memorial was established through a partnership between the Kigali City Council and the Aegis Trust. Remains were brought from across the capital — from streets, rivers, and shallow graves — and interred in mass graves in lots of 100,000. The memorial includes a Wall of Names that continues to grow as victims are identified. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

name: Murambi Genocide Memorial — Nyamagabe, Southern
type: National Memorial & UNESCO World Heritage Site
desc: A former technical school where an estimated 45,000–65,000 Tutsi were directed by authorities under false promises of French military protection. Water and food were cut off before the attack. Preserved mummified remains bear witness to the scale of the atrocity.

testimony.text: They told us the French soldiers would protect us at the school. Thousands walked for hours to reach it. When we arrived, there was no water. No food. We grew weaker every day. Then on the night of the twenty-first, they came. I survived because I was buried under others. I carry them with me in every breath.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor accounts, Murambi memorial records

context: The Murambi Technical School was still under construction in April 1994 when local officials directed Tutsi civilians there, claiming French troops would provide protection. After days without provisions, soldiers and Interahamwe militia attacked on the night of April 21. The memorial, founded in 1995, displays preserved remains in the former classrooms. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.

name: Bisesero Genocide Memorial — Gisovu, Karongi
type: Memorial of Resistance & UNESCO World Heritage Site
desc: Known as the "Memorial of Resistance," honoring the Tutsi community of Bisesero who organized armed defense of the hills for over two months before being overwhelmed. Of an original community exceeding 50,000, approximately 1,500 survived.

testimony.text: We fought with stones, with sticks, with anything we could find. Every day they came, and every day we fought. For sixty-two days we held the hills. When the French soldiers finally arrived, they said they would return to help. They came back three days later. In those three days, thousands more of us died. We were the Hill of Resistance. We are still standing.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts of Bisesero resistance, multiple survivor testimonies

context: Bisesero's hills saw the longest sustained resistance of the genocide. The Tutsi community, with a historical tradition of self-defense, organized themselves against militia and military forces from April through late June. French forces from Operation Turquoise made initial contact on June 27 but delayed their return, during which thousands more were killed. The memorial has nine buildings representing the nine former communes of Kibuye Province. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.

name: Nyamata Genocide Memorial — Bugesera, Eastern
type: National Memorial & UNESCO World Heritage Site
desc: A Catholic church in Bugesera district, 35 km from Kigali, where over 10,000 people seeking sanctuary were killed. The church preserves bloodstained clothing, personal belongings, and human remains. The iron door still bears machete scars.

testimony.text: I was a child when we ran to the church. My mother told me that God would protect us in His house. When they broke through the iron door, I hid under the bodies. I could hear everything. I lay there for two days before I moved. The clothes hanging in that church — those were worn by people I knew. By my family. This church is their voice now.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented child survivor testimony, Nyamata memorial records

context: The Nyamata Catholic Church served as a traditional place of refuge for the Tutsi community of Bugesera, which had experienced periodic persecution since 1959. When the genocide began, thousands gathered at the church. On April 14–15, 1994, militia and soldiers broke through the reinforced iron doors and massacred those inside and in the surrounding grounds. The memorial, preserving the church as it was found, was established in 1997. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.

name: Ntarama Genocide Memorial — Bugesera, Eastern
desc: A former Catholic church 1 km from Nyamata, preserved exactly as it was found. The floor contains bones intermingled with clothing, shoes, and personal items. Approximately 5,000 people were killed here.

testimony.text: The church at Ntarama was small, but we believed we would be safe inside. They came with grenades first, then machetes. When you walk in today, you walk on the floor where we fell. The bones you see were people who sang hymns on Sunday. People who shared food with their neighbors. Do not look away. They deserve to be seen.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor accounts, Ntarama memorial records

context: Ntarama Church, located in Bugesera district just 1 km from Nyamata, was one of the first genocide memorials established in Rwanda in 1995, with the support of the genocide survivors' organization Ibuka. The memorial preserves the church interior as it was found after the massacre, including human remains, clothing, and personal effects.

name: Nyarubuye Genocide Memorial — Kirehe, Eastern
desc: A former Catholic church, convent, and school of the Benebikira Sisters. Approximately 20,000 people were killed at this site, making it one of the largest individual massacre locations.

testimony.text: Nyarubuye was supposed to be different. The parish had always been a safe place. When the killing started, people came from every direction — from the hills, from the valleys. By the time the journalists arrived weeks later and showed the world what happened here, there was no one left to tell them. I tell it now because I am one of the few who can.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented witness accounts, Nyarubuye memorial archives

context: Nyarubuye parish in the Eastern Province became one of the first massacre sites documented by international media, when journalists arrived weeks after the killings. The compound held an estimated 20,000 people who had gathered from the surrounding hills. The attack began on April 15 and continued for several days.

name: Nyange Church Memorial — Kivumu, Rutsiro
desc: Located in the Western Province, a site where Tutsi sought refuge before being attacked. The memorial honors those who perished and serves as a place for community remembrance.

testimony.text: At Nyange, we had no weapons. We had only each other and our faith. When they demolished the walls onto us, we held hands. I felt the weight of the building and the weight of every person I had ever known. Some of us were pulled out. Most were not.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, CNLG memorial records

context: The Nyange memorial site commemorates one of many massacres in the Western Province where Tutsi civilians gathered at churches and public buildings.

name: Kibuye Genocide Memorial — Karongi, Western
desc: Near Lake Kivu, honoring the estimated 12,000 victims killed at Gatwaro Stadium and surrounding sites in Kibuye prefecture.

testimony.text: Kibuye was beautiful. The lake, the hills, the churches. They used our trust in these places against us. When the prefect told us to gather at the stadium for our own safety, we believed him. We had always believed the authorities. That belief killed us.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor testimony, Kibuye region

context: Kibuye prefecture in the Western Province experienced among the highest proportional death tolls during the genocide. Local authorities directed Tutsi civilians to gather at Gatwaro Stadium and churches, claiming it was for their protection.

name: Rebero Genocide Memorial — Kicukiro, Kigali
desc: Located on Rebero hill in Kigali, this memorial commemorates both Tutsi civilians and political figures who were targeted or who bravely opposed the genocide.

testimony.text: On Rebero hill, they killed politicians who refused to participate. They killed leaders who said no. These were people with the power to run, to hide, to leave the country. They stayed. They said no. And they were killed for it. We remember their courage here.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented historical records, Rebero memorial

context: The Rebero memorial uniquely honors both civilian victims and political figures who resisted the genocide. An estimated 14,400 people are interred at the site.

name: Nyanza-ETO Genocide Memorial — Kicukiro, Kigali
desc: Located at the former ETO school in Kicukiro district. When UN peacekeepers withdrew on April 11, thousands of civilians were marched to Nyanza hill and massacred.

testimony.text: The soldiers — the blue helmets — they were our only hope. When they started packing their vehicles, a silence fell over all of us. Mothers stopped singing to their children. We watched them drive away. Then we were marched to the hill. On April 11th every year, I stand on that hill and I remember what it means to be abandoned by the world.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts of the ETO/Kicukiro withdrawal

context: The Nyanza memorial at the ETO (École Technique Officielle) in Kicukiro commemorates one of the most documented failures of international intervention. Belgian UNAMIR peacekeepers were ordered to withdraw on April 11, abandoning approximately 4,000 civilians.

name: Mugombwa Genocide Memorial — Gisagara, Southern
desc: Located in the Southern Province, commemorating victims from the Gisagara district area.

testimony.text: In Mugombwa, the hills that had fed us became the hills that hid us. But they searched every hill. Every valley. Every home. The memorial stands where we could not.
testimony.attribution: Based on community memorial records, Southern Province

context: The Mugombwa memorial commemorates victims from the Gisagara district, part of the former Butare prefecture. Killings intensified after the replacement of the moderate Tutsi prefect in mid-April 1994.

name: Bigogwe Genocide Memorial — Nyabihu, Northern
desc: Located in the Nyabihu district near the Virunga mountains, this memorial honors victims from the highlands region.

testimony.text: We lived in the shadow of the volcanoes. The mountains that had always protected us could not protect us from our neighbors. At Bigogwe, we remember that geography cannot save you from ideology.
testimony.attribution: Based on community records, Bigogwe area

context: Bigogwe, in the highlands near the Virunga volcanoes, was a site where Tutsi communities in the remote mountainous region were systematically targeted.

name: Busogo Genocide Memorial — Musanze, Northern
desc: Located in the Northern Province near Musanze, commemorating victims from the northern highlands.

testimony.text: In the north, near the mountains, people thought the killing would not reach us. It reached us. It reached everywhere.
testimony.attribution: Based on community memorial records, Northern Province

context: The Busogo memorial commemorates victims from the northern highlands near Musanze district.

name: Butare University Memorial — Huye, Southern
desc: At the National University of Rwanda in Butare, commemorating students, faculty, and intellectuals who were targeted.

testimony.text: The university was where we came to build Rwanda's future. Tutsi professors, Tutsi students — we studied together, we ate together. Then they were told to separate us. Our classmates pointed us out. Knowledge could not save us. But remembering them honors what they were building.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts from the National University of Rwanda

context: The National University of Rwanda in Butare was the country's premier academic institution. When the genocide reached Butare after the prefect's replacement on April 19, Tutsi faculty and students were specifically targeted.

name: Muyumbu Genocide Memorial — Rwamagana, Eastern
desc: Located in the Rwamagana district, commemorating victims killed along the main eastern road corridor from Kigali.

testimony.text: Muyumbu was on the road east from Kigali. The roadblocks caught everyone trying to flee the capital. There was nowhere to run that did not have a checkpoint, a barrier, a list.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Eastern Province records

context: Muyumbu, along the main road east from Kigali toward Rwamagana, was a site where roadblocks intercepted Tutsi civilians fleeing the capital.

name: Mutete Genocide Memorial — Karongi, Western
desc: Located in the Western Province hills, commemorating victims from the Karongi district area.

testimony.text: In the hills of Mutete, people tried to organize resistance like in Bisesero. But we were fewer. We had less time. The memorial marks where ordinary people tried to become heroes and were cut down.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Western Province records

context: The Mutete memorial commemorates victims from the Karongi district area. Killings were coordinated with the broader Kibuye prefecture massacres.

name: Belgian Peacekeepers Memorial — Camp Kigali, Nyarugenge
desc: Commemorates the ten Belgian UNAMIR paratroopers of the 2nd Para-Commando Battalion (KIBAT) tortured and killed at Camp Kigali on April 7, 1994. Their murder prompted Belgium's full withdrawal from UNAMIR, fatally weakening the international force.

testimony.text: We watched them come for the soldiers. We had trusted those men with our lives. The Belgian soldiers had been protecting us outside the Prime Minister's residence when they were taken away. When Belgium announced it was pulling out, we understood what that meant. We were alone. Completely alone.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts of the Camp Kigali events, April 7 1994

context: Ten Belgian paratroopers assigned to protect Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana were seized by Rwandan Presidential Guard soldiers on the morning of April 7 and taken to Camp Kigali, the national gendarmerie headquarters. They were brutally killed. The killings were later found to have been deliberate acts aimed at prompting Belgian withdrawal. Belgium announced its full UNAMIR withdrawal within days, removing the most capable contingent of the peacekeeping force.

name: Cyanika Parish Memorial — Nyamagabe, Southern
desc: Located near the Burundi border in Nyamagabe district, the Cyanika parish memorial commemorates thousands of Tutsi who fled to the church and surrounding area seeking safety and were massacred in April 1994.

testimony.text: We had walked for two days to reach Cyanika. People said the border was close, that maybe we could cross into Burundi. But the parish was as far as we got. When they came, we had nowhere left to run. I survived because I fell and was covered. The memorial is for the ones who did not get up.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor accounts, Nyamagabe district records

context: Cyanika, in the southern reaches of Nyamagabe district close to the Burundi border, was one of several parish-based massacre sites in what was formerly Gikongoro prefecture. Thousands of Tutsi from surrounding communes converged on the site in early April. Local authorities and militia coordinated the attack. The memorial was established to honor victims from multiple surrounding communes.

name: Gahanga Genocide Memorial — Kicukiro, Kigali
desc: Located in Kicukiro district at the southern edge of Kigali, the Gahanga memorial commemorates victims from the sector who were killed as the genocide spread outward from the capital's center in April 1994.

testimony.text: Gahanga was a quiet place. People had gardens, small farms. The killings came street by street, hill by hill. There was a pattern to it — they knew who lived where. The lists had been prepared long before April 6. At Gahanga we remember that this was not chaos. It was organized. It was deliberate.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Kicukiro district memorial records

context: Gahanga sector in Kicukiro district became one of many sites on Kigali's outskirts where systematic killings took place as Interahamwe and Presidential Guard units moved outward from the city center. The memorial serves the communities of southern Kigali and was established with support from local survivor organizations.

name: Gashirabwoba Memorial — Bushenge, Nyamasheke
desc: Located in Nyamasheke district near Lake Kivu, the Gashirabwoba memorial honors victims from the lakeshore communities of the Western Province who had no escape route when the killings reached their area.

testimony.text: The lake was right there. People tried to swim. Some drowned. Some were killed in the water. The shore became a place of death, not refuge. For the people of Gashirabwoba, there was nowhere to go.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Nyamasheke district memorial records

context: Communities along the western shore of Lake Kivu in Nyamasheke district were caught between the killings on land and the open water of the lake. The Gashirabwoba memorial was established to honor victims from this lakeshore area, where geography offered no escape.

name: Kaduha Parish Memorial — Nyamagabe, Southern
desc: The Saint-Pierre de Kaduha Catholic parish in Nyamagabe district was one of the largest single massacre sites in the Southern Province. Thousands of Tutsi from surrounding communes gathered at the church and were attacked by militia and soldiers.

testimony.text: At Kaduha, the priests tried to protect us. They stood in front of us. It did not matter. When men arrive with guns and machetes and a list, faith and courage are not enough. Ten thousand people came to God's house to be saved. Most of them died there. I carry the weight of every name I remember.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor testimony, Kaduha parish memorial records

context: Saint-Pierre de Kaduha parish in Nyamagabe district (formerly Gikongoro prefecture) received Tutsi refugees from numerous surrounding communes beginning in early April 1994. Despite the presence of local clergy, militia and military forces attacked the compound. An estimated 10,000–15,000 people were killed at the site over several days. The memorial was established with support from the Diocese of Butare and the Rwandan government.

name: Kibeho Genocide Memorial — Nyaruguru, Southern
desc: Located in Nyaruguru district near the well-known Catholic Marian shrine, the Kibeho memorial honors Tutsi victims from the area killed during the genocide. The shrine grounds and surrounding hills became sites of mass killing.

testimony.text: Kibeho was a place of pilgrimage. People came here from all over Rwanda to pray. When the killing began, we thought the Virgin would intercede. We prayed. The killers came anyway. The shrine that had drawn people to this hill became the place where they were slaughtered on it.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor accounts, Nyaruguru district records

context: Kibeho in Nyaruguru district is internationally known as the site of Marian apparitions recognized by the Catholic Church. During the genocide in 1994, thousands of Tutsi gathered at the shrine seeking protection. They were massacred. The same area later saw the 1995 Kibeho camp massacre when Rwandan forces killed thousands of Hutu IDPs. The genocide memorial specifically honors the 1994 Tutsi victims.

name: Mugonero Genocide Memorial — Gishyita, Karongi
desc: The Mugonero Adventist Hospital complex in Karongi district, where thousands of Tutsi seeking refuge were massacred on April 16, 1994. Notable for a letter from Tutsi pastors to their church president requesting protection, and his refusal.

testimony.text: The letter we wrote to the church president said: we are due to be killed on Saturday with our families. We ask you to intercede for us. He wrote back that the time had come when those who must die, must die. We read that letter and we understood. Even our own church had abandoned us. They killed us in the hospital where we had come to be healed.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts including the Mugonero letter, April 1994
testimony.source: Genocide Archive Rwanda / Adventist Church records

context: The Mugonero Adventist complex — comprising a hospital, church, and school — in Bwishyura sector, Karongi district (formerly Kibuye) was led by Seventh-day Adventist church president Elizaphan Ntakirutimana. When Tutsi pastors wrote to him requesting help on April 15, he refused and later led attackers to the compound. On April 16, militia and soldiers killed an estimated 8,000 people. Ntakirutimana was later convicted of genocide by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

name: Musanze Genocide Memorial — Musanze, Northern
desc: The principal genocide memorial for Musanze district (formerly Ruhengeri), commemorating victims from Rwanda's northern volcanic highlands region, where killings were particularly intense given the area's proximity to RPF strongholds.

testimony.text: Ruhengeri was RPF country — that is what they said. So the Tutsi here were doubly suspect. Doubly targeted. They did not just kill us because we were Tutsi. They killed us because they said we were RPF collaborators. The accusations were false. The killings were real.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor accounts, Musanze district records

context: Musanze district (formerly Ruhengeri prefecture) in northern Rwanda was strategically sensitive during the genocide given its proximity to the RPF's northern front and the Virunga mountains. The Hutu Power authorities used the perceived threat of RPF invasion to intensify killings of local Tutsi. The Musanze memorial commemorates victims from across the district and serves as the primary memorial site for the Northern Province's most populous district.

name: Mvuzo Genocide Memorial — Rulindo, Northern
desc: Located in Rulindo district in Rwanda's Northern Province, the Mvuzo memorial commemorates victims from the rolling hills of the former Byumba prefecture, where killings spread rapidly from Kigali northward.

testimony.text: We heard what was happening in Kigali on the radio. We thought it would not come here. Three days later, the roadblocks appeared. Our neighbors who had farmed beside us for twenty years suddenly had machetes. Some of them looked away when we were taken. That is the worst memory — not the hatred, but the silence of those who said nothing.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented survivor accounts, Rulindo district records

context: Rulindo district, in the northern province between Kigali and Musanze, experienced killings that followed the pattern established in the capital: roadblocks, lists, and coordinated attacks on Tutsi gathering points. The Mvuzo memorial serves communities in the western part of Rulindo district.

name: Ngororero Genocide Memorial — Ngororero, Western
desc: Located in Ngororero district in the Western Province, this memorial honors victims from the former Kibuye-Gitarama border area, a region that experienced systematic violence as the genocide radiated outward from Kigali.

testimony.text: Ngororero sits between Kigali and Kibuye. The killers came from both directions. We were caught in the middle with nowhere to run. The memorial here is for people who had nowhere to go and no one who came to help them.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Ngororero district memorial records

context: Ngororero district occupies the hilly terrain between Kigali and Kibuye, along former administrative boundaries. The area saw coordinated violence as the genocide spread both from the capital eastward and from the Kibuye prefecture massacres westward. The district memorial honors victims from across Ngororero's sectors.

name: Nyamasheke Genocide Memorial — Kagano, Nyamasheke
desc: Located in Nyamasheke district on the shores of Lake Kivu, this memorial honors victims from the southwestern communities of the Western Province. The lakeshore geography trapped many civilians with no avenue of escape.

testimony.text: We lived by the lake all our lives. We knew its rhythms. When the killing began, some people tried to use boats to reach the DRC shore. Some made it. Many were killed in the water or on the shore before they could board. The lake that had given us fish gave us nothing else. The memorial stands at the water's edge, looking west, toward where some of us tried to go.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Nyamasheke district memorial records

context: Nyamasheke district sits along the southwestern shore of Lake Kivu, bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo. During the genocide, the lake represented both a potential escape route and a death trap. Many Tutsi civilians attempted to cross by boat to the DRC, with mixed results. Coordinated attacks by Interahamwe and local officials prevented most escapes. The Nyamasheke memorial was recognized within the UNESCO World Heritage nomination process.

name: Nyundo Seminary Memorial — Rubavu, Western
desc: Located near the Grand Séminaire de Nyundo in Rubavu district, the memorial commemorates victims from the Gisenyi area including students, clergy, and civilians killed when attacks reached the Diocese of Nyundo's institutions.

testimony.text: Nyundo had a seminary, a cathedral, schools. It was a center of faith and learning for the whole region. When the militia arrived, they did not spare priests or seminarians. They had lists. They checked identities at the door. Being educated, being ordained, being loved — none of it protected you. The memorial at Nyundo is for those who believed that civilization would protect them.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts of the Nyundo seminary attacks
testimony.source: Genocide Archive Rwanda / Diocese of Nyundo records

context: The Grand Séminaire de Nyundo in Rubavu district (formerly Gisenyi prefecture) was a major Catholic diocesan institution near Lake Kivu and the DRC border. When the genocide began, the seminary and surrounding area became a target as Interahamwe sought Tutsi students, clergy, and community members. Several priests and seminarians were killed. The Nyundo memorial honors victims from the Rubavu area including those connected to the diocese's institutions.

name: Ruhanga Genocide Memorial — Kicukiro, Kigali
desc: Located in Kicukiro district at the eastern edge of Kigali, the Ruhanga memorial honors victims from the sector who were killed as militia systematically moved through the city's outer neighborhoods in April and May 1994.

testimony.text: By the time they reached Ruhanga, we had already heard what was happening in the center of the city. We had days of terror before they arrived. Waiting is its own kind of violence. The memorial here is for people who spent days knowing what was coming and could not stop it.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Kicukiro district memorial records

context: Ruhanga sector in Kicukiro district lies on the eastern periphery of Kigali. As militia and soldiers systematically moved outward from the city center, outer neighborhoods like Ruhanga were targeted in the second and third weeks of the genocide. The memorial was established with support from local survivor associations and the Kicukiro district authorities.

name: Rusiga Genocide Memorial — Rulindo, Northern
desc: Located in Rulindo district in the Northern Province, the Rusiga memorial commemorates victims from the northern hills who were targeted in the weeks following the genocide's outbreak in Kigali.

testimony.text: Rusiga is up in the hills. We thought distance would protect us. The killers walked for hours to reach us. They had lists prepared months before. They knew exactly who to find. The memorial reminds us that the genocide was not spontaneous — it was planned, and even the remotest hills were on the plan.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Rulindo district memorial records

context: Rusiga sector in Rulindo district occupies hilly terrain in northern Rwanda between Kigali and the Byumba region. The area saw killings that followed the structured pattern of the wider genocide: roadblocks, identity checks, coordinated militia attacks on Tutsi gathering points. The Rusiga memorial serves communities in northern Rulindo.

name: Jabana Genocide Memorial — Gasabo, Kigali
desc: Located in Gasabo district northeast of Kigali city center, the Jabana memorial commemorates victims from a sector that saw coordinated attacks as the genocide spread outward from the capital in the opening days of April 1994.

testimony.text: Jabana was close enough to the city that we could hear the gunfire on April 7. By the 9th the Interahamwe were in our sector. They had come from Kigali, organized, with weapons that had been stored for weeks. We were their next assignment. The memorial at Jabana is for ordinary families who became targets of a plan they never knew was being made against them.
testimony.attribution: Based on documented accounts, Gasabo district memorial records

context: Jabana sector in Gasabo district lies northeast of Kigali and was targeted in the early phase of the genocide as organized militia moved outward from the city. Local Interahamwe units, equipped and organized through months of preparation, carried out systematic attacks on Tutsi households and gathering points. The memorial honors victims from Jabana and surrounding Gasabo areas.
